content: Pagoda dogwood, scientifically known as Cornus alternifolia and commonly referred to as alternate-leaved dogwood, is a deciduous tree native to eastern North America. Its range extends from Newfoundland to southern Manitoba and Minnesota, and southward to northern Florida and Mississippi. This species typically grows to a height of 8 meters, occasionally reaching up to 10 meters, with a trunk diameter of up to 15 centimeters. The branches are arranged in distinctive horizontal layers, separated by gaps, giving the tree a tiered appearance. The leaves of the pagoda dogwood are elliptic to ovate in shape, measuring 4–12 cm in length and 2–6 cm in width. Unlike most other species in the Cornus genus, the leaves are alternately arranged along the stems rather than in opposite pairs. They often cluster densely at the ends of twigs, creating an almost whorled appearance. The upper surface of the leaves is smooth and green, while the underside is hairy and bluish in color. The bark of the tree is gray to brown, becoming ridged as the tree matures. The flowers of Cornus alternifolia are small, cream-colored, and consist of four petals. The tree produces fruit in the form of blue-black drupes, approximately 8–10 mm in diameter. These fruits are tipped with a remnant of the style and are borne in October. Pagoda dogwood is often found along forest margins, beneath open deciduous canopies, or near the edges of swamps. It thrives in moist, well-drained soils. The tree is valued for its ornamental qualities, particularly its wide-spreading, tiered branches and flat-topped crown. Unlike the flowering dogwood (Cornus florida), the pagoda dogwood lacks the large white bracts surrounding its flower clusters, and its fruit is dark purple with a strong, unpleasant aromatic flavor. The bark of the tree is dark reddish-brown with shallow ridges, while the young branchlets are initially pale reddish-green, maturing to a darker green. The wood is reddish-brown with pale sapwood, and it is heavy, hard, and close-grained, with a specific gravity of 0.6696 and a weight of 41–73 pounds per cubic foot. The winter buds are light chestnut brown and pointed. As the buds grow, the inner scales enlarge and reach about half an inch in length before falling off. The leaves emerge from the buds in an involute manner, initially reddish-green on the upper surface and coated with silvery-white tomentum on the underside. When fully developed, the leaves are bright green above and pale, downy, and nearly white beneath. The leaves are feather-veined, with a broad, yellowish midrib and approximately six pairs of primary veins. In autumn, the foliage turns yellow or a combination of yellow and scarlet. The petioles are slender, grooved, and hairy, with clasping bases. The flowers bloom in April and May. They are perfect (bisexual) and cream-colored, borne in many-flowered cymes at the ends of short lateral branches. The calyx is cup-shaped, and the four petals are valvate in bud, opening to reveal oblong petals with rounded ends. The stamens, which are four in number, are exserted with long, slender filaments. The anthers are oblong, introrse, versatile, and two-celled, with the cells opening longitudinally. The pistil consists of an inferior ovary with two cells, a columnar style, and a capitate stigma. The fruit is a globular drupe, blue-black in color, measuring about one-third of an inch in diameter. It is tipped with the remnant of the style, which rises from a slight depression. The nut within the drupe is obovoid and has multiple grooves.
